summary: Research nuclear program mechanics, deterrence/brinkmanship design, historical numbers, and UI for the nuclear pillar

reports.topic: How strategy games model nuclear weapons acquisition, and a concrete program-chain design (stages, inputs, timescales, decisions) for a 1950-start Cold War grand strategy game where total war is the failure state

findings.name: Why HoI4's classic nuke chain is forgettable — and why Paradox itself rebuilt it in 2024
findings.detail: Old HoI4 (per https://hoi4.paradoxwikis.com/Nuclear_weapons): research 3 techs in a line, build reactor buildings, then passively drip 1 bomb per 852 days per reactor (thermonuclear: 1 per 1,278 days). Zero decisions after the unlock, zero world reaction to acquiring them, zero interaction with economy/espionage/diplomacy, and the payoff is tactical province damage that arrives after the war is already decided. It is a progress bar you forget you started. The strongest evidence that this design fails: Paradox replaced it in the Götterdämmerung expansion (Nov 2024) with Special Projects (https://hoi4.paradoxwikis.com/Special_project) — named scientists with skill levels and traits (diminishing returns for stacking them), dedicated Nuclear Research Facilities that consume supply and can be damaged/raided (pausing progress — counterplay!), 90-day prototype iterations that make progress visible and lumpy, 'breakthrough' points partly obtainable by capturing enemy facilities, and a project chain (Reactor → Commercial Reactor / Fission Bomb → Thermonuclear). Every element they added — staffed facilities, visible stages, espionage interaction, sabotage vulnerability — is a lesson about what the old system lacked.
findings.recommendation: Do not ship 'research tech, build building, wait N days per bomb.' Build the program as a staffed, sited, staged industrial project with visible milestones, spy-observable signatures, and sabotage counterplay from day one. Treat HoI4's 2024 rework as the floor, not the ceiling — it still lacks economy-scale inputs (electricity, uranium logistics) that our game already simulates.

findings.name: Survey of the rest of the genre: one good idea each, and two cautionary tales
findings.detail: Civilization's Manhattan Project: a named, world-announced threshold project gated on the uranium strategic resource — its virtue is milestone clarity (everyone knows what it means when it completes), its flaw is that nothing interesting happens between start and finish. Twilight Struggle (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twilight_Struggle): abstracts acquisition away entirely because the game is about escalation control; its DEFCON track makes whoever triggers DEFCON 1 lose immediately — the definitive 'nuclear war = you lose' mechanic, but it models USE, not acquisition. Terminal Conflict (https://store.steampowered.com/app/745970/Terminal_Conflict/): Doomsday Clock tension meter, 'balance the world on the brink of mutually assured destruction to ensure total victory' — arsenal building is present but shallow. ICBM: Escalation (https://store.steampowered.com/app/2647680/ICBM_Escalation/): tech-era research plus construction of subs/bombers/ICBMs with escalation pacing modes — arsenal as unit production, no program drama. SuperPower 2 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SuperPower_2): nukes as a tech-level checkbox bought with money; critics called the whole game 'a ponderous spreadsheet' — the cautionary tale for stat-slider acquisition. Supreme Ruler Cold War (https://store.steampowered.com/app/73220/Supreme_Ruler_Cold_War/): research tree + minister-managed production; nukes exist but are buried in the spreadsheet with no narrative beats. Realpolitiks is the same pattern smaller. Nobody in the genre has shipped an acquisition chain that is itself a game.
findings.recommendation: Steal exactly one thing from each: Civ's world-event milestone framing, Twilight Struggle's 'crossing the line loses the game' escalation philosophy for use, ICBM's separation of warheads from delivery systems — and avoid the SP2/Supreme Ruler failure mode where the program is a menu, not a story.

findings.name: The Manhattan Project was >80% industrial plant, not science — so the program belongs to the economy pillar
findings.detail: Of the ~$1.9B total cost, over 80% went to building and operating fissile-material production plants, not weapons design; peak workforce ~130,000, with Oak Ridge alone at 82,000 by May 1945; authorization to Trinity took 3 years 1 month (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan_Project). K-25 alone cost $479.6M, employed 25,000 construction workers, and was the largest building on earth (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-25). Games get this backwards: they make the bomb a research-tree leaf when historically the physics was the cheap part and the separation plants were the nation-bending expense. This is why a research-tab implementation always feels weightless.
findings.recommendation: Cost the program primarily in industrial capacity, construction, electricity, and labor (we have province demography — facility sites need workforce), with research/scientists as a smaller gating input. The player should feel the program competing with tanks, consumer goods, and reconstruction for the same industrial points. Monthly budget draw hangs off SimClock::new_month.

findings.name: Enrichment is electricity-monstrous — a made-to-order hook for our regional power grids
findings.detail: K-25 required its own dedicated 238 MW coal power plant (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-25); the 1950s Portsmouth gaseous diffusion plant peaked at 2,100 MW and 18 billion kWh/year (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portsmouth_Gaseous_Diffusion_Plant) — single facilities drawing a meaningful fraction of a regional grid. No strategy game has ever modeled this, and we already have regional electricity grids in the sim. Crucially, this is also the detection mechanic: a nation that suddenly builds gigawatts of generation next to a remote desert site is telling every intelligence service what it is doing — power-grid expansion is the observable signature of a 'secret' HEU program.
findings.recommendation: Make an Enrichment Complex consume a large, visible share of its regional grid (order of 15–25% of a typical region's 1950 capacity per level). Insufficient grid power throttles fissile output proportionally (integer math: output = base × min(supplied, demanded)/demanded). Foreign intel estimates of enemy programs should partly key off observed grid buildout — feeding the existing fuzzed-estimate display language.

findings.name: The route choice (plutonium vs HEU) is the program's central strategic decision, with opposite cost/physics/signature profiles
findings.detail: Historically real and historically agonized-over: Britain chose plutonium because 'a reactor could be built more cheaply than a separation plant that produced an equivalent quantity of enriched uranium' — a diffusion plant alone was £30–40M against £44M for their entire weapons-facility program 1946–53 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Explosive_Research). The USSR initially judged U-235 enrichment 'hopeless' and went plutonium via the Mayak reactors (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_atomic_bomb_project). The US, uniquely rich, ran five separation technologies and both bomb types in parallel (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan_Project). The tradeoff matrix: Plutonium route = cheaper, modest electricity, but requires production reactors + reprocessing plant AND the harder implosion weapon design (extra design-project risk); HEU route = brutally expensive and electricity-hungry but permits the simple gun-type design that needs no test to be credible. Signatures differ too: reactors emit detectable signatures and need cooling water siting; enrichment emits grid load.
findings.recommendation: Stage 2 of the chain is an explicit, mostly-irreversible route choice presented as a choice event with advisor arguments. Pu route: Production Reactor + Reprocessing Plant facilities, low grid draw, must complete an 'Implosion Design' sub-project (scientist-gated, failure-prone without espionage data). HEU route: Enrichment Complex, huge grid draw and 2–3× industrial cost, no design risk. Superpowers may run both in parallel at ~1.8× total cost. This one decision differentiates US/USSR/UK/France/China playthroughs automatically.

findings.name: Uranium sourcing is geopolitics, not mining — Shinkolobwe and Wismut make ore access a foreign-policy and covert-ops objective
findings.detail: In 1950 Shinkolobwe (Belgian Congo) held roughly half the world's known uranium reserves, with freak 65% ore against a 0.3% post-war viability threshold; it was erased from maps, closed to journalists, and garrisoned (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shinkolobwe). The USSR, locked out of the Congo, depended on satellite mines: in 1950, East Germany's Wismut delivered 1,224 t and Czechoslovakia (Joachimsthal) 281 t against only 417 t domestic Soviet production, dug substantially by forced labor (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_atomic_bomb_project). The West ran the Combined Development Trust precisely to corner global supply and deny it to Moscow. We already have uranium deposits (including Shinkolobwe and Joachimsthal) in the resource layer — the design should make access to them contested, not a passive +N.
findings.recommendation: Fissile production requires uranium feed (t/month) from controlled deposits or import agreements. Make denial a first-class play: covert ops to sabotage or interdict enemy ore shipments, diplomacy/influence to flip supplier states, a 'preclusive purchasing' money-sink action. A USSR player should feel the Congo lockout; a Western player should watch Wismut's tonnage in intel reports. Losing uranium feed stalls the enemy program without firing a shot — perfect below-the-threshold gameplay.

findings.name: Espionage as breakthrough accelerant: the Fuchs effect is worth ~2 years and de-risks design
findings.detail: Kurchatov said stolen Manhattan Project material 'adds exactly what we have been missing,' accelerating the Soviet program by an estimated two full years, and — as important — espionage proved implosion with reactor plutonium would work, letting the USSR skip dead ends (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_atomic_bomb_project). HoI4's rework gestures at this with facility-capture breakthroughs (+10%, decaying) but has no ongoing spy-vs-program game. This is the natural bridge between our intelligence pillar and the nuclear pillar: penetration of an enemy program should both reveal its true state (unfuzzing the estimate) and be stealable as design data.
findings.recommendation: A successful long-term penetration of an enemy nuclear program yields (a) sharpened intel estimates and (b) a stackable 'stolen design data' modifier: −20–35% duration on design sub-projects and removal of first-test fizzle risk. Counterintelligence sweeps can burn the network with a public spy-trial event (tension bump, propaganda value). Historical seasoning: Fuchs was arrested January 1950 — a ready-made early scripted event for our start date.

findings.name: Secrecy vs speed is a real dial, and detection has a beautiful historical mechanic: atmospheric sampling
findings.detail: Britain hid its program from most of the Cabinet and Parliament, announcing it only via 'an oblique answer to a pre-arranged question,' and drew staff quietly at civil-service salaries — slow but silent (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Explosive_Research). The US detected RDS-1 within days via WB-29 airborne fallout sampling despite total Soviet secrecy — meaning tests are undeniable public events even when conducted in secret, while programs before testing are hideable but leaky (grid buildout, procurement, scientist disappearances). And crash programs are loud: Beria's forced-labor, secret-city approach traded observability and internal risk for speed (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_atomic_bomb_project).
findings.recommendation: Give the program a 3-position posture: Covert (0.7× speed, low monthly detection accrual), Standard (1.0×), Crash (1.5× speed, high detection accrual, accident-event risk, morale/consumer-goods penalty). Detection is a monthly deterministic accumulator (SimRng-forked rolls) fed by grid signature + procurement volume + enemy penetration; crossing thresholds upgrades the rival's intel estimate tier. First detonation is ALWAYS detected within days regardless of posture — fallout sampling — and fires a global teletype event.

findings.name: Scientists as a named, scarce, stealable resource — but with diminishing returns
findings.detail: Kurchatov and Penney were single points of failure; Penney's team grew from a planned 220 to 500 by 1948 and Aldermaston peaked at ~4,000 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Explosive_Research). HoI4's implementation (skill levels, traits like Nuclear Specialist, each additional scientist contributing 0.5× the previous — explicit diminishing returns) is genuinely good and worth copying (https://hoi4.paradoxwikis.com/Special_project). Named scientists also create covert-ops targets (defection, assassination — both historical: the game should let players run an Operation Paperclip and fear an enemy one) and intel flavor for the teletype presentation.
findings.recommendation: Model 5–15 named scientists per nuclear-capable nation (historical where sourced via the historian agent, generic elsewhere), with an integer skill 1–5. Program speed multiplier = f(sum of skills with 0.5× stacking decay). Scientists are recruitable, defectable, and assassinatable via the covert-ops layer; losing your program head costs months. Keep it small — a roster, not a spreadsheet.

findings.name: Recommended program chain: six stages, four inputs, calibrated to historical timescales
findings.detail: Historical calibration: US crash program 3.1 years with unlimited money; USSR ~4 years post-Hiroshima with espionage and forced labor; UK 5.7 years (decision Jan 1947 → Hurricane Oct 1952) on £44M austerity budget; France ~6, China ~9. So in-game: a superpower crash program ≈ 4 game-years, a determined middle power ≈ 6–8 — long enough that starting one is a defining campaign decision, short enough to pay off in a 1950–1970 campaign. At 1950 start: US has a small arsenal, USSR has tested (Aug 1949) with fissile production scaling, UK is mid-program (stage 3–4) — three different onboarding states for free. INPUTS: money (monthly draw), industrial capacity (construction + steady consumables), electricity (grid share, HEU route especially), uranium feed (t/month from deposits/imports), scientists, and optionally stolen data. STAGES: (0) Found Program — secret choice event, sets funding tier + posture; (1) Research Establishment — site it (region choice matters: workforce from province demography, remoteness vs sabotage), recruit scientists; milestone 'first pile critical' (internal event, spy-detectable); (2) Route Choice — Pu vs HEU vs both (see route finding); (3) Fissile Production — facilities come online, integer kg/month into stockpile, throttled by uranium feed × power satisfaction × scientist factor; visible to the player as a production line, visible to enemies as fuzzed estimates; (4) Weaponization & First Test — at ~1 warhead-equivalent of material, choose: TEST (global wire event, permanent tension shift, deterrence credibility unlocked, program public) or STOCKPILE UNTESTED (secret, but zero deterrence value and fizzle risk retained — untested bombs deter no one); (5) Arsenal & Follow-ons — warheads/month scaling with facilities; thermonuclear program repeats stages 1–4 in miniature (breakthrough physics + a test that is its own bigger world event, cf. Ivy Mike/Castle Bravo); delivery systems (bombers now, missiles later) are a separate procurement chain so 'has bombs' ≠ 'can deliver them', which ICBM: Escalation gets right.
findings.recommendation: Implement stages as explicit sim states per nation (BTreeMap keyed by CountryTag), advanced on new_month, all quantities integer (kg fissile, MW, tons ore). Every stage transition fires an event — internal choice events for the owner, teletype intel events for rivals at their current estimate fidelity. Numbers live in tuning modules/RON per the conventions. The player's decision list — found/fund/site/route/posture/steal/test/thermonuclear — is eight real decisions, which is eight more than HoI4 classic offered.

findings.name: Integration with the tension meter: acquisition milestones move the world, and testing is itself an escalation decision
findings.detail: Twilight Struggle's core insight — the player who triggers nuclear war loses immediately (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twilight_Struggle) — matches our 'total war is the failure state' north star, but it only governs use. The acquisition-side corollary: every PUBLIC nuclear milestone should shift the global tension baseline and rewrite everyone's options. RDS-1's detection in Sept 1949 transformed US policy within months (NSC-68). A first test is simultaneously the program's triumphant payoff, a permanent +tension event, the moment deterrence begins working for you, and the moment you become a targeting priority — the best kind of ambivalent reward. Untested-but-suspected programs should generate crisis events (demands for inspections, preventive-strike temptations for rivals), making the pre-test window the most dangerous phase — historically true (US planners debated preventive war 1949–54) and mechanically rich.
findings.recommendation: Wire milestones to the existing 0–100 tension meter: first fission test +5–8 global tension and a band-check; first thermonuclear +8–12; arsenal size thresholds shift crisis-event weightings. Deterrence value = f(tested designs × deliverable warheads as ESTIMATED by the rival, not actual count) — so the fuzzed-intel layer directly determines whether deterrence holds, and a player can run bluffs or be victims of enemy overestimates. This makes the nuclear program the load-bearing connector between all four pillars rather than a bolt-on.

key_takeaways: HoI4's classic nuke system fails because acquisition is a decisionless passive drip (1 bomb/852 days) with no world reaction, no economy interaction, and no counterplay — and Paradox's own 2024 Götterdämmerung rework (named scientists, raidable facilities, prototype stages, breakthrough theft) is a public admission of exactly which ingredients were missing. Sources: https://hoi4.paradoxwikis.com/Nuclear_weapons , https://hoi4.paradoxwikis.com/Special_project

Historically the bomb was an industrial-economic undertaking, not a research unlock: >80% of the Manhattan Project's ~$1.9B went to fissile-material plants (130k workers), and enrichment plants individually drew hundreds to thousands of MW (K-25: dedicated 238 MW plant; Portsmouth: 2,100 MW peak). Our regional power grids, province demography, and uranium deposits mean we can model this authentically where no other game could. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan_Project , https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-25 , https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portsmouth_Gaseous_Diffusion_Plant

The three genuinely strategic decisions inside a program are route (cheap Pu + hard implosion physics vs expensive power-hungry HEU + easy gun-type — the choice Britain and the USSR each agonized over), uranium access (Shinkolobwe held ~half of known 1950 reserves; the USSR lived off Wismut/Joachimsthal tonnage — sourcing and DENIAL are foreign-policy and covert-ops gameplay), and secrecy posture (crash = fast but loud; espionage stole the USSR ~2 years). Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Explosive_Research , https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shinkolobwe , https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_atomic_bomb_project

Recommended chain: six stages (Found → Establishment+scientists → Route choice → Fissile production → Test-or-stockpile decision → Arsenal/thermonuclear follow-on), inputs of money/industry/electricity-share/uranium-feed/scientists, integer kg-per-month production advanced on monthly ticks, calibrated so a superpower crash takes ~4 game-years and a middle power 6–8 (matching US 3.1y / USSR ~4y / UK 5.7y / France ~6 / China ~9).

The first test must be the game's signature world event: always detected within days via atmospheric sampling regardless of secrecy (as RDS-1 was in 1949), delivered on the teletype, permanently shifting the tension meter — and deterrence should key off the RIVAL'S fuzzed estimate of your tested, deliverable arsenal rather than the true count, making the intel layer, the tension meter, the economy, and the program one connected system. Twilight Struggle's 'whoever triggers DEFCON 1 loses' remains the right philosophy for the use side. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twilight_Struggle

Anti-patterns to avoid: nukes as tech-level checkbox purchasable with money (SuperPower 2 — 'a ponderous spreadsheet'), nukes buried in minister-managed production with no narrative beats (Supreme Ruler Cold War), and milestone projects with nothing interesting between start and completion (Civilization's Manhattan Project). Every stage transition in our chain should fire an event someone cares about.

reports.topic: How nuclear weapons matter without being used: deterrence mechanics, the cost of first use, and nuclear-war-as-failure end states — with concrete recommendations for a 0-100 tension-meter Cold War sim

findings.name: Twilight Struggle's DEFCON: the meter matters because ordinary play degrades it and it restricts your action space
findings.detail: Three interlocking rules make TS's DEFCON the genre masterpiece ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twilight_Struggle)): (1) aggressive-but-normal actions (coups in battleground countries) each degrade DEFCON one step — danger is a byproduct of doing the thing you want to do, not a separate 'press the red button' choice; (2) each DEFCON level progressively LOCKS OUT regions from coups/realignments (at DEFCON 2 only Africa/Latin America remain), so tension physically shrinks the playable map; (3) 'If DEFCON 1 is reached during a player's action round, that player is deemed to have caused a nuclear war and loses immediately' — attribution: the mover, not the world, eats the loss. Plus Required Military Operations: you LOSE victory points each turn if you don't conduct military ops at least equal to current DEFCON — domestic hawks force you toward the cliff you're trying to avoid. DEFCON also improves 1 step at the start of each turn, creating a breathing rhythm of crisis and détente. The dread of playing at DEFCON 2 — where one miscalculated card ends you — is the emotion players cite as the best in board gaming.
findings.recommendation: Port all three rules to the tension meter. (1) Make routine aggressive actions (coups, border incidents, blockades, shoot-downs) mechanically ADD tension as a side effect — never a separate abstract 'raise tension' button. (2) Give each tension band hard action locks AND unlocks: high bands forbid direct-confrontation actions in core theaters (Europe) while low bands forbid nothing; conversely some coercive actions only become AVAILABLE at high tension. (3) Attribution rule: the actor whose action pushes tension across the war threshold is the one who 'started it' — they take the failure screen, the blame in the epitaph, and (in scored terms) the loss. (4) Add a hardliner-pressure system: each faction's domestic hawks demand periodic demonstrations of resolve; ignoring them costs political power/legitimacy, satisfying them costs tension. This is the engine that makes staying at tension 20 impossible and staying below 90 the actual game.

findings.name: Balance of Power: the crisis subgame — escalate or back down, with prestige as the currency of humiliation
findings.detail: Crawford's design ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balance_of_Power_(video_game))) reduces brinkmanship to a discrete crisis ladder: a provocation opens a crisis, each side alternately escalates (diplomatic note → military maneuvers → higher rungs) or backs down; backing down costs prestige (the victory metric), so both sides have real reasons not to yield; misjudging the opponent's resolve ignites nuclear war. The famous end screen: 'You have ignited a(n accidental) nuclear war. And no, there is no animated display of a mushroom cloud with parts of bodies flying through the air. We do not reward failure.' Blank screen, game over, no spectacle. The genius is that every crisis is a game of chicken where the information you need most — how much the opponent actually cares — is uncertain.
findings.recommendation: Build a discrete CRISIS object on top of the continuous tension meter, delivered through the existing teletype/wire-service choice-event engine (perfect aesthetic match — crises SHOULD arrive as flash traffic). A crisis has: a subject (Berlin, a shot-down aircraft, missiles in Cuba), a ladder of 4-6 named rungs (protest → mobilize → blockade → ultimatum → strike), a hidden AI resolve value the player only sees as a fuzzed intelligence estimate (reuse the 2-sig-fig range display — 'CIA assesses Soviet resolve: FIRM'), and stakes. Each rung climbed adds tension and raises the stakes; backing down ends the crisis but costs prestige/alignment proportional to how high the ladder got — backing down from rung 4 is a Cuba-style humiliation that shifts third-world alignment and can crack your bloc. Time-box rungs in ticks (48-72 in-game hours to respond) so real-time pressure exists but stays deterministic. Most of the game's nuclear content should live here, in crises where nukes are never fired.

findings.name: Deterrence math: model first-strike capability vs second-strike survivability, and compute stability from BELIEVED numbers, not true ones
findings.detail: The core deterrence relation ([Second strike, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_strike)): stability exists when each side's arsenal can survive a surprise attack and still deliver unacceptable retaliation; vulnerable arsenals create 'use them or lose them' pressure that makes crises unstable. Survivability comes from dispersal, hardened silos, SSBNs, bombers on alert, early warning. Counterforce (striking weapons) vs countervalue (striking cities) targeting is the other axis. Historically, in 1950 the US had ~300 bombs and no ICBMs, the USSR had ~5 and tested its first in Aug 1949 — and both sides' ESTIMATES of each other were wildly wrong (bomber gap, missile gap), which is exactly what the game's intelligence-estimate display language models.
findings.recommendation: Arsenal model (integer math, fits the sim): per-nation stockpile of warheads, each assigned to a delivery leg (bombers → later missiles → later SSBNs) with per-leg survivability and penetration percentages, both improvable by tech/posture. Derive two numbers per dyad: FirstStrikeDamage (what I destroy of your arsenal if I go first) and AssuredRetaliation (warheads you land on me after absorbing my best first strike). Deterrence holds when AssuredRetaliation ≥ an 'unacceptable damage' threshold. THE KEY DESIGN MOVE: the AI and the player each compute this from intelligence ESTIMATES (fuzzed ranges from the existing intel system), not truth. Espionage (U-2 overflights, moles, atomic spies) narrows the range; deception/dispersal widens it. A 'crisis stability' indicator per dyad — stable (both have assured retaliation), unstable (someone has use-it-or-lose-it pressure) — should feed event weights: unstable dyads at high tension spawn preemption-temptation and false-alarm events. This makes the intel pillar and the nuclear pillar the same pillar: the game of not knowing how many bombs the other side really has IS the 1950s.

findings.name: Tactical nukes are the designed trap: seemingly usable, actually the top of a slide (Princeton's Plan A)
findings.detail: Princeton SGS's [Plan A simulation](https://sgs.princeton.edu/the-lab/plan-a) — built from real force postures — shows a single tactical 'warning shot' escalating through tactical exchange → strategic counterforce → city-targeting, with 90+ million dead and injured within the first few hours. The policy point: 'limited' nuclear use is a fiction because each use creates overwhelming pressure to respond in kind, one rung up. Historically this is exactly the 1950 question — MacArthur requested atomic weapons for Korea; Truman's refusal helped establish the nuclear taboo ('tradition of non-use') that is arguably the most important norm of the whole Cold War.
findings.recommendation: Mechanically distinguish tactical from strategic use. Tactical use should be OFFERED, temptingly, by the event engine at moments of conventional desperation (Korean War slice collapsing, Chinese intervention, MacArthur demanding the bomb) with a real, visible battlefield payoff — it genuinely wins the battle. Its true cost is systemic and mostly irreversible: (1) tension +25-40 instantly (into the top band); (2) the NUCLEAR TABOO breaks — a global one-way flag that permanently cheapens all future use for everyone (AI use-thresholds drop; every later crisis has nuclear rungs), so the world you 'saved' Korea in is a far more dangerous world forever; (3) alignment collapse — neutrals and even allies shift away hard (India, Scandinavia, Japan react to Hiroshima's shadow); (4) the opponent draws a retaliation choice-event with in-kind-or-worse options. Strategic use against homeland targets is not an action at all in the normal UI — it exists only as the terminal rung of a crisis ladder, behind a deliberately heavy confirmation, and is understood to be pulling the whole temple down.

findings.name: HoI4's fizzle: why 'nuke as damage multiplier' kills the fantasy
findings.detail: In HoI4 ([wiki](https://hoi4.paradoxwikis.com/Nuclear_weapons)) a nuke does 10-90% strength/org damage in a province, wrecks buildings, costs the defender up to 20% war support, and (post-rework) leaves 1-2 years of fallout debuffs. That's it. No deterrence, no retaliation mechanic, no political consequence beyond a war-support tick, no reason NOT to use one the moment it's built. The wiki's deterrence section is empty because the mechanic has none. Result: players stockpile nukes as siege artillery and the single most consequential decision in 20th-century statecraft plays like a strategic bombing option. It fails because HoI4 models the bomb's PHYSICS and skips its POLITICS — and because in a total-war game there is no peace left to lose.
findings.recommendation: Hard rule for the design doc: a nuclear weapon is never a unit order; it is always a political event. No 'nuke province' button on the map. Physical effects (which the province/demography model can do brutally well — real populations mean real, named death tolls per city) are the CHEAP part; every use must pass through the choice-event engine where the costs are diplomatic, tension-based, and irreversible. The game's advantage over HoI4 is exactly that its failure state is total war — so the bomb can threaten something the player actually holds: the peace.

findings.name: DEFCON (Introversion) and First Strike: if the war happens, everybody dies — score it in megadeaths and make winning feel like losing
findings.detail: DEFCON's subtitle is literally 'Everybody Dies' ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defcon_(video_game))): scoring is enemy megadeaths minus your own losses, presented in clinical WOPR-style vector graphics — the horror comes from the dissonance between the calm interface and the numbers. Its first-strike timing dance (launching reveals silos; mode-switching is slow) is a real retaliation-window calculation. First Strike ([Steam](https://store.steampowered.com/app/587000/First_Strike/)) makes whole nuclear wars playable in 30-60 minutes to show 'how little it takes to heat things up' — an explicitly cautionary framing. Terminal Conflict ([Steam](https://store.steampowered.com/app/745970/Terminal_Conflict/)) contributes the Doomsday Clock as ambient countdown dread and the design goal of 'balancing the world on the brink of mutually assured destruction to ensure total victory' — i.e., riding the meter high on purpose is a strategy.
findings.recommendation: Steal three things. (1) Brinkmanship must PAY: in crises, the side with higher demonstrated resolve (recent tension-raising actions, alert level, arsenal edge) extracts concessions more cheaply — high tension is coercive leverage, which is why players will voluntarily climb toward the failure state. That's the chicken dynamic the whole pillar needs. (2) Alert postures as the mid-game verb: raising alert (bombers dispersed/airborne, later missiles fueled) improves survivability and crisis leverage but adds tension and — critically — raises the deterministic probability weight of accident/false-alarm events rolled from SimRng at high bands (Able Archer, Petrov, the training-tape incident). Deterrence stability should decay the longer both sides sit at maximum alert. (3) If the exchange comes, present it in the teletype voice: clinical wire copy, city names from the real demography data, casualty integers. No explosions rendered on the map — just strike reports scrolling.

findings.name: The end state: nuclear war is a failure screen, not a game phase — Crawford's rule, executed with the game's own data
findings.detail: Three convergent precedents: Crawford's blank screen ('We do not reward failure'), Twilight Struggle's instant attributed loss at DEFCON 1, and DEFCON's pyrrhic megadeath ledger where even the winner has lost most of their population. All three refuse to make post-exchange play interesting; the fantasy-fulfillment version (Fallout-style aftermath gameplay) would reward the failure and undermine the entire staying-below-the-threshold premise. The one refinement the board game adds over Crawford is ATTRIBUTION — someone specific caused it — and the one refinement DEFCON adds is ACCOUNTING — the cost is enumerated, not abstract.
findings.recommendation: Full strategic exchange = immediate, irreversible campaign end. No aftermath gameplay, no loading-screen mushroom cloud glamour. The end screen is a final wire-service transmission that goes silent: datelined bulletins for the first strikes, then integer casualty totals computed from the REAL province demography ("LONDON — NO FURTHER TRANSMISSIONS"), then attribution — which leader crossed which rung, quoted from the actual event log — then a single line of score-as-epitaph: the date, i.e., how many years the player kept the peace ('The peace held for 11 years, 4 months'). Tactical use is survivable (that's the trap); the failure state triggers only on strategic homeland exchange or on tension pegging 100 during an unresolved crisis. And one anti-frustration rule Twilight Struggle teaches by counterexample ('DEFCON suicide' via trap cards): the threshold must never be crossable by hidden or forced effects — only by an explicit choice the player (or AI) made with the consequence labeled. The dread comes from choosing, not from being ambushed by bookkeeping.

findings.name: The 1950 start is a gift: the arsenal is an economic project the existing systems already support
findings.detail: In January 1950 the US has a few hundred fission bombs and SAC bombers; the USSR tested RDS-1 five months ago and has a handful; the H-bomb decision (Truman, Jan 31, 1950 — thirty days into the campaign) hasn't happened; Klaus Fuchs is arrested Feb 2, 1950. The game already has uranium deposits (Shinkolobwe supplied the Manhattan Project; Joachimsthal fed the Soviet program), regional electricity grids (Oak Ridge's gaseous diffusion plants consumed on the order of 1% of US electricity), industry, and province demography. Every ingredient of an arsenal-as-supply-chain model is on the board.
findings.recommendation: Make warheads a production chain, not a research unlock: uranium provinces → enrichment/reactor sites that draw heavily on a specific regional grid → warheads/year, all visible on the map and therefore SPYABLE and SABOTAGEABLE (covert-ops pillar) and BOMBABLE-in-conventional-war. Stockpiles are secret; the opponent sees only the fuzzed 2-sig-fig estimate, which their espionage improves and your security/deception degrades — letting the game recreate the bomber/missile gaps as emergent intel failures. Key early-game choice events fall out of history for free: the H-bomb decision (accelerate the arms race for deterrence weight vs restraint), atomic-spy scandals, whether to put Shinkolobwe under guard. The pillar's early game is thus about BUILDING deterrence and STEALING the truth about the other side's — nuclear gameplay with zero detonations.

key_takeaways: Danger must be a byproduct of desirable actions (Twilight Struggle): coups, incidents, and alerts should ADD tension as a side effect, tension bands should lock/unlock whole categories of action, and domestic hardliner pressure should punish sitting safely at low tension — that loop, not the bomb itself, is the flagship mechanic.

Build a discrete crisis-ladder subgame (Balance of Power) on top of the continuous meter, delivered via the existing teletype event engine: escalate-or-back-down rungs, hidden AI resolve shown only as fuzzed intel estimates, prestige/alignment loss for backing down that scales with how high the ladder climbed, and time-boxed responses in ticks.

Deterrence math = FirstStrikeDamage vs AssuredRetaliation per dyad, computed from intelligence ESTIMATES rather than true stockpiles — merging the nuclear and intel pillars: espionage narrows the range, deception widens it, and 'use it or lose it' instability should drive preemption-temptation and false-alarm events at high tension.

Tactical nukes are the designed trap (Plan A): offered at moments of conventional desperation with a real battlefield payoff, but costing a tension explosion (+25-40), permanent global taboo-break flag that cheapens all future use, alignment collapse among neutrals and allies, and an opponent retaliation event. Strategic use exists only as the terminal rung of a crisis ladder.

Never model the bomb as a unit order (HoI4's failure): no nuke button on the map — every use is a political choice event whose real costs are diplomatic and irreversible; physical damage is the cheap part.

Nuclear war is an immediate, attributed, anticlimactic failure state (Crawford/TS/DEFCON): campaign ends, final wire transmission enumerates megadeaths from real province demography and names who crossed the last rung, score is simply how long the peace held — and the threshold must only ever be crossable by an explicit, labeled choice, never hidden bookkeeping.

The 1950 start makes the arsenal an economic-espionage object: uranium → grid-hungry enrichment → secret stockpiles seen by the enemy only as fuzzed ranges, recreating the bomber/missile gaps emergently and giving the pillar a rich early game with zero detonations.

reports.topic: Sourced historical data for tuning a 1950-start nuclear weapons system: stockpiles, economics, infrastructure, delivery, decision points, and intelligence accuracy

findings.name: 1. Warhead stockpiles 1945-1965: exponential US growth, USSR a decade behind, tiny third parties
findings.detail: Canonical dataset: Norris & Kristensen, 'Global nuclear weapons inventories, 1945-2010', Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists 66(4), July 2010 (the NRDC Nuclear Notebook lineage). Five-year anchors verified against the Wikipedia table citing that paper (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_nuclear_weapons_stockpiles_and_nuclear_tests_by_country): US 1945: 2, 1950: 299, 1955: 2,422, 1960: 18,638, 1965: 31,149. USSR 1945: 0, 1950: 5, 1955: 200, 1960: 1,605, 1965: 6,129. UK 1955: 14, 1960: 42, 1965: 436. France: 0 until first test Feb 13 1960; 32 by 1965. China: first test Oct 16 1964; ~5 by 1965. Intermediate years from the same dataset (from my knowledge of the paper — treat as ±10%): US 1946: 9, 1947: 13, 1948: 50, 1949: 170, 1951: 438, 1952: 841, 1953: 1,169, 1954: 1,703, 1956: 3,692, 1957: 5,543, 1958: 7,345, 1959: 12,298 (note the 1958-59 leap — sealed-pit mass production), 1961: 22,229, 1962: 25,540. USSR 1949: 1, 1951: 25, 1952: 50, 1953: 120, 1954: 150, 1956: 426, 1957: 660, 1958: 869, 1959: 1,060, 1961: 2,471, 1962: 3,322. Critical nuance for a 1950 start: the US '299' figure counts weapons whose cores sat in AEC civilian custody, unassembled; assembly took ~2 days per Mark 4 and only a few dozen assembly teams existed. Usable-on-day-one arsenals in Jan 1950 were far smaller than stockpile numbers imply. US doubling time 1948-1958 was roughly every 2 years; the USSR tracked the US curve with an ~8-10 year lag until the late 1960s.
findings.recommendation: Tune production curves so an unconstrained-historical US run yields ~300 warheads in Jan 1950 and ~2,400 by 1955, USSR ~5 and ~200 — i.e., a 60:1 ratio at game start collapsing to ~12:1 by 1955. Model 'stockpile' and 'assembled/ready' as separate numbers in 1950-1955 (assembly teams as a bottleneck resource); the sealed-pit transition (~1957) is a tech that removes the distinction and unlocks the 1958-59 style production explosion. Third parties: UK gets single digits from 1953, France/China contribute nothing before 1960/1964 — do not give them meaningful arsenals in the game's first decade.

findings.name: 2. Program economics: nation-scale entry cost, then cheap warheads whose real cost is fissile material
findings.detail: Manhattan Project total through Dec 1946: $1,889,604,000 then-year dollars (~$21.6B in 1996$), per Brookings' Atomic Audit cost tables (https://www.brookings.edu/the-costs-of-the-manhattan-project/), of which Oak Ridge alone was $1.19B (63%!) and Hanford $390M — versus only $74M for Los Alamos. The science was cheap; ISOTOPE SEPARATION was the money. Peak workforce ~125,000-130,000 (K-25 site alone peaked at 25,266 construction workers in May 1945, per fetched Wikipedia/official history); ~500,000 people cumulatively. Soviet program: Stalin gave it 'greatest priority' post-Hiroshima (decree of Aug 20 1945 creating Beria's Special Committee); scale estimates run 300,000-700,000 workers including Gulag labor at the mining and construction sites (Holloway, 'Stalin and the Bomb', 1994) — uncertainty flagged: no reliable ruble cost figure exists. Per-weapon cost early 1950s: dominated by fissile material, not hardware. Schwartz (ed.), 'Atomic Audit' (Brookings, 1998) puts total US spending on warhead R&D+production 1940-1996 at ~$409B (1996$) for ~70,000 warheads built — a long-run average near $5-6M each, but early-1950s marginal cost was mostly the several kg of Pu/HEU per core (Hanford/Savannah River production cost of plutonium ran on the order of tens to low hundreds of $ per gram — flag: exact per-gram figures vary by accounting method). Delivery always cost more than warheads: B-36 flyaway ~$4.1M, B-52 ~$14.4M (1955$), and Atomic Audit attributes 56% of total US nuclear spending to delivery vs ~7% to the bombs themselves.
findings.recommendation: Price the SYSTEM, not the bomb: an enrichment/reactor complex should cost the equivalent of a full year of great-power military-industrial output and take 3-4 game-years to build (Manhattan: Sept 1942 groundbreaking to Jul 1945 test); once built, each warhead should be cheap — its real cost expressed as fissile-material throughput, electricity, and a small industry tick. Make delivery systems cost 5-10x the warheads they carry so the player's budget fight is bombers/missiles, not bombs. Soviet program should be purchasable at ruinous opportunity cost (the historical USSR did it during postwar famine years 1946-47).

findings.name: 3. Production infrastructure: your electricity grid and uranium deposit systems ARE the nuclear system
findings.detail: Electricity: wartime Oak Ridge is famously cited as consuming ~1% of all US electricity (more than wartime NYC); by the mid-1950s the AEC's three gaseous-diffusion complexes (K-25/Oak Ridge; Paducah KY, operating 1952; Portsmouth OH, 1954-56) drew on the order of 6-12% of US electrical output — the AEC was the nation's largest single power consumer, with dedicated multi-GW plants (e.g., ~1.5-2 GW blocks at Paducah and Portsmouth). Flag: the 1% Oak Ridge figure is ubiquitous but loosely sourced; the mid-50s aggregate is variably given as 6.7 GW / '~10%' in Hewlett & Holl's official AEC history and Atomic Audit — use the range, not a point value. Savannah River (5 heavy-water reactors, first critical Dec 1953, ~$1.3B, built by DuPont for the H-bomb tritium/Pu surge) is the expansion play. Soviet equivalents: Chelyabinsk-40/Mayak (first production reactor 'A' critical June 19 1948), Sverdlovsk-44 enrichment, Arzamas-16 (Sarov) design lab — same shape, built with penal labor. Uranium 1945-1955 (verified via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shinkolobwe and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wismut_(mining_company)): US supply was overwhelmingly FOREIGN — Shinkolobwe (Belgian Congo) ore ran up to 65% U3O8 (vs ~0.2-0.5% typical), shipped ~400 tons oxide/month from late 1942, and postwar deliveries of 1,440 t (1947), 2,792 t (1951), 1,600 t (1953) of concentrate; plus Canadian Eldorado. USSR: Joachimsthal (Czechoslovakia) and above all Wismut in East Germany — over 200,000 workers at peak (autumn 1950!) and 230,400 t U total 1947-1990, the early bomb program's ore backbone before Soviet domestic deposits (Kazakhstan, Fergana) came online mid-1950s.
findings.recommendation: Gate warhead production on three existing game systems: (a) a regional-grid electricity draw so large it visibly starves civilian industry — an enrichment complex should demand ~1-10% of a superpower's national generation, making grid expansion a real strategic decision; (b) named uranium sources as chokepoints — Shinkolobwe supplying the US and Wismut/Joachimsthal supplying the USSR are covert-ops and diplomacy targets (Congo instability, Czech coup Feb 1948, East German control), and losing one should stall the curve for years; (c) reactor-years as the plutonium clock (first Soviet reactor criticality Jun 1948 → first test Aug 1949 = ~14 months from criticality to bomb). This turns the flagship pillar into gameplay over systems already built.

findings.name: 4. Delivery timeline: for the whole 1950s, having bombs is not the same as being able to deliver them
findings.detail: US: Silverplate/Saddletree B-29s (combat radius ~1,600 mi; only 46 nuclear-capable aircraft as late as 1946-47, per Norris et al.); B-36 (service 1948, ~380 built, ~3,400 mi combat radius — first true intercontinental bomber); B-47 (service 1951, 2,032 built — the backbone, but only ~2,000 mi radius, hence the forward-base ring in UK/Morocco/Spain/Guam and KC-97 tankers); B-52 (service Feb 1955, 744 built by 1962, ~8,800 mi unrefueled). SAC in Jan 1950: ~520 bombers, mostly B-29/B-50, under Curtis LeMay since Oct 1948. USSR: Tu-4 (reverse-engineered B-29, first flight May 1947, ~850 built) could reach CONUS only on ONE-WAY missions — the USSR had effectively zero two-way strike capability against the US homeland until Tu-95 'Bear' (first flight Nov 1952, service 1956, ~15,000 km range) and the small M-4 Bison force (only 93 built, ~19 ever on nuclear alert — see finding 6; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bomber_gap); Tu-16 Badger (1954) covered Europe/Asia only. ICBMs: R-7 first successful flight Aug 21 1957, Sputnik Oct 4 1957, but as a weapon it was terrible — cryogenic fueling took many hours, launch sites were soft and few (combat duty Feb 1960, never more than ~4-6 operational pads; actual Soviet ICBM count in early 1961 was FOUR, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missile_gap). US Atlas D operational Sept 1959; Polaris A-1 SLBM: USS George Washington sailed the first deterrent patrol Nov 15 1960 with 16 missiles of 1,200 nmi range — the first survivable second-strike leg.
findings.recommendation: Model delivery capability as its own tech/procurement track with a range-vs-basing check against the province map: in 1950 the USSR should be able to threaten Europe/Japan but hit CONUS only via one-way Tu-4 raids (a distinct, desperate order type with crew loss), while the US needs its overseas base network — making bases diplomatic/covert-ops objectives. Early ICBMs should be scripted as prestige+terror weapons with awful readiness (hours to launch, vulnerable pads) so bombers stay relevant through 1960; Polaris ends first-strike calculus and should measurably damp the escalation meter's usefulness as a coercion tool once deployed.

findings.name: 5. Decision points 1950-1955 map directly onto the existing choice-event engine
findings.detail: (a) Jan 31 1950: Truman approves the H-bomb after the NSC Special Committee (Acheson, Johnson, Lilienthal) recommendation, overriding the GAC's Oct 30 1949 majority report (Oppenheimer et al.) which opposed the 'Super' on moral/strategic grounds; Klaus Fuchs' espionage confession (Jan 27 1950) landed days before. Payoff chain: Ivy Mike Nov 1 1952 (10.4 Mt), Soviet 'layer-cake' Joe-4 Aug 12 1953 (400 kt), true Soviet two-stage RDS-37 Nov 22 1955 (1.6 Mt). (b) Korea: Truman's Nov 30 1950 press conference stating atomic use was under 'active consideration' (caused Attlee to fly to Washington Dec 4-8); Dec 24 1950 MacArthur submitted a list of retardation targets (he later claimed wanting 26-34 bombs); Apr 6 1951 Truman authorized transfer of 9 complete Mark 4 bombs to military custody and B-29 deployment to Guam — days before firing MacArthur Apr 11 (documented in the National Security Archive's Korea nuclear briefing books; Roger Dingman, 'Atomic Diplomacy during the Korean War', International Security 13:3, 1988). (c) Castle Bravo Mar 1 1954: predicted ~6 Mt, yielded 15 Mt (lithium-7 miscalculation); contaminated the Lucky Dragon No. 5 crew and Rongelap, ignited the worldwide fallout/test-ban movement. (d) 'Massive Retaliation': NSC 162/2 adopted Oct 30 1953 (the New Look — nuclear weapons 'as available for use as other munitions'), Dulles speech Jan 12 1954. (e) Open Skies: Eisenhower's proposal at the Geneva summit Jul 21 1955; Khrushchev rejected it as espionage — followed by the actual espionage answer, the U-2 (first Soviet overflight Jul 4 1956).
findings.recommendation: Ship these five as authored teletype event chains with genuine branches: the H-bomb decision as the 1950 opener (decline = Soviet thermonuclear lead by 1953 and a domestic-politics hit; accept = tension bump + GAC resignations flavor); Korea atomic-transfer as the flagship escalation-band test where the meter, custody rules, and ally reactions (Attlee event) all interact; Castle Bravo as a semi-random test-outcome event (yield overshoot chance on new designs) that permanently spawns a world-opinion/test-ban pressure track; New Look as a doctrine choice trading conventional force cost for a lower nuclear-use threshold; Open Skies as an intel-pillar crossover offering transparency vs. the U-2 covert path with shoot-down risk.

findings.name: 6. Intelligence accuracy: the historical record is systematic OVER-estimation of the enemy — your fuzzed-range UI should be biased, not just noisy
findings.detail: Three documented failures, all in the same direction after 1949: (a) First Soviet test: 1948-49 US estimates (ORE 3-49) put the most probable date at mid-1953; the actual test was Aug 29 1949, detected by WB-29 air sampling Sept 3 — an UNDER-estimate, the last one. (b) Bomber gap: extrapolating from a July 1955 Aviation Day flyby in which 10 M-4 Bisons looped around and flew past again with 8 more, NIEs projected ~800 Bisons by 1960 (Nov 1957 NIE: 150-250 by 1958, 600+ by mid-60s); actual production was 93 airframes ever, ~19 on nuclear alert — an overestimate near 10x, deflated by U-2 imagery from 1956 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bomber_gap). (c) Missile gap: NIE 11-10-57 (Dec 1957) projected first Soviet ICBM capability 1958-59; NIE 11-5-58 (Aug 1958) allowed 100 ICBMs by 1960 and 500 by 1961-62; the true number in early 1961 including prototypes was 4. Corona satellite imagery (first success Aug 1960, analyzed Jan 1961) killed the gap; the Sept 1961 NIE cut the estimate to 'no more than 25' and McNamara conceded no gap in Feb 1961 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missile_gap). Note the mechanism in each case: a single deliberate Soviet deception or displayed capability, multiplied by worst-case Air Force extrapolation — and the inflated numbers drove real US procurement (the B-52 and Minuteman buys were justified by phantom fleets). Soviet estimates of the US were far more accurate thanks to espionage (Fuchs gave them the Fat Man design and US production data through 1949).
findings.recommendation: Extend the existing 2-sig-fig fuzzed-estimate display with a BIAS term, not just a range: enemy stockpile/delivery estimates should trend 2-10x high by default, tightening only when the player invests in collection (U-2-equivalent 1956+, satellite recon 1960+), each with its own crisis risk (U-2 shootdown May 1 1960 as the cautionary event). Give the AI (and player) a deliberate 'parade deception' covert action that inflates the opponent's estimate of your forces — historically it worked, and it provoked the arms race, so it should raise opponent build rates and tension: deterrence value now, arms-race blowback later. Asymmetry: successful espionage penetration (Fuchs-style) collapses the target's estimate error to near-truth AND accelerates the spy's own program by 1-2 years, which is exactly what it did for the USSR.

key_takeaways: Use Norris & Kristensen (Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, 2010) as the single canonical stockpile dataset: US 2→299→2,422→18,638 and USSR 0→5→200→1,605 across 1945/50/55/60; at game start the ratio is 60:1 and the USSR runs ~8-10 years behind the US curve — verified anchors at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_nuclear_weapons_stockpiles_and_nuclear_tests_by_country.

The bomb's real economy is infrastructure, not units: 63% of the Manhattan Project's $1.89B went to Oak Ridge isotope separation alone (Brookings, https://www.brookings.edu/the-costs-of-the-manhattan-project/), enrichment complexes drew ~1% (wartime) to ~6-12% (mid-1950s) of US electricity, and 1940s-50s uranium came from a handful of named foreign chokepoints (Shinkolobwe at 65% ore grade; Wismut with 200,000 workers) — so the game's nuclear system should be built ON the existing grid, industry, and uranium-deposit systems, with warheads as cheap outputs of expensive plants.

Delivery lags warheads by years and is the more expensive half (56% vs 7% of US nuclear spending per Atomic Audit): the USSR cannot two-way-strike CONUS until ~1956-57, early ICBMs were near-useless as weapons (4 real Soviet ICBMs in early 1961), and Polaris (Nov 1960) is the survivability breakpoint — model delivery as its own range-vs-basing track that keeps overseas bases and bombers strategically central through 1960.

Historical intelligence error was directionally biased overestimation (bomber gap ~10x, missile gap ~25-100x, per the NIE record at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missile_gap and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bomber_gap) and deception caused it — so the fuzzed-estimate UI should carry a hidden bias term, deception should be a playable covert action with arms-race blowback, and this loop is the cleanest bridge between the intelligence pillar and the escalation pillar.

Five dated, sourced decision points (H-bomb Jan 31 1950; Korea atomic custody transfer Apr 6 1951; Castle Bravo Mar 1 1954; NSC 162/2 / Massive Retaliation Oct 1953-Jan 1954; Open Skies Jul 21 1955) give the scripted-event engine a ready-made 1950-55 spine where each choice trades tension-meter position against capability — reinforcing the north star that the system exists to keep the player below the threshold, not to fight the war.

reports.topic: Presentation of nuclear programs, arsenals, and alert states in games/film, and a concrete UI recommendation for the game's nuclear layer

findings.name: The canon converges on one image: a dark big board where everything reads at a glance
findings.detail: Every touchstone resolves to the same fantasy. Introversion's DEFCON uses a 1980s vector-map aesthetic explicitly 'reminiscent of the big boards that visually represented thermonuclear war in Dr. Strangelove, Fail-Safe, and especially WarGames'; critics called it 'one of the best-looking PC games of the year' and 'worth it for the presentation alone' ([Wikipedia: Defcon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defcon_(video_game))). WarGames' NORAD displays were real vector graphics — Colin Cantwell's animations on HP 1345A monochrome vector displays, rear-projected live so actors saw them ([Wikipedia: WarGames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WarGames)); the WOPR prop was styled after 1940s-50s military tabulating machines and consoles — exactly this game's period. Ken Adam's War Room in Dr. Strangelove is the other pole: a black reflective floor, giant wall maps with aircraft tracks, and a green-baize circular table lit by a ring of lamps because Kubrick wanted the actors to feel they were 'playing a game of poker for the fate of the world' ([Wikipedia: Dr. Strangelove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dr._Strangelove)). The lesson: the nuclear layer should not be a menu — it should be a place. Fallout's contribution is tonal, not layout: the deadpan bureaucratic framing of apocalypse, which this game's teletype/dossier identity already owns.
findings.recommendation: Build 'THE BOARD' as a dedicated map mode + docked console, not a window. Entering nuclear view darkens the whole map to near-black, provinces become thin phosphor outlines (single accent hue per bloc), and all normal UI chrome dims. Aircraft/missile tracks render as slow vector arcs with trailing afterglow, WOPR-style. Oswald for the big status words, Courier Prime for everything data. This mode IS the flagship-pillar identity shot — it should be the game's key art.

findings.name: Twilight Struggle's DEFCON track: dread comes from a marker the player owns that mechanically tightens the game
findings.detail: In Twilight Struggle, DEFCON degrades one step per battleground coup, each step geographically restricts where coups/realignments are legal, and 'if DEFCON 1 is reached during a player's action round, that player is deemed to have caused a nuclear war and loses immediately' ([Wikipedia: Twilight Struggle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twilight_Struggle)). The dread is physical (a marker sliding toward a labeled doom box) and mechanical (options visibly close off as it moves). Crucially, YOU can be the one who ticks it to 1 — the loss is attributed, not ambient. The existing 0-100 global tension meter is the ambient half; it lacks the attributed, chunky, restriction-bearing half.
findings.recommendation: Keep the continuous 0-100 tension as the underlying sim variable, but PRESENT it through its bands as a 5-position stepped track with hard edges — a physical marker that visibly clunks between labeled boxes, each band printed with what it unlocks/forbids (e.g. band 4: covert ops in enemy sphere draw double tension; band 2: conventional attacks on nuclear powers risk automatic escalation rolls). When an action would push tension across a band edge, the confirmation dialog must say so: 'THIS ACTION MOVES THE WORLD TO CONDITION 2.' Attribution is the point: the ticker should record which nation's action caused each band change, and the failure screen should name it.

findings.name: Own program: exact milestones as a stamped classified dossier, gated by systems the game already has
findings.detail: The player's own program should be perfectly legible — the contrast with fuzzy enemy estimates is itself the design statement. Historical program structure gives natural milestones: uranium supply (the game already models Shinkolobwe/Joachimsthal deposits), enrichment/separation plant (a massive electricity sink — Oak Ridge's gaseous diffusion was one of the biggest power consumers in the US, mapping directly onto the regional electricity-grid system), weapon design, device assembly, test. US intelligence expected the Soviet bomb in 1953; it arrived in 1949 ([Wikipedia: RDS-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RDS-1)) — which shows milestones are also the things enemy spies steal.
findings.recommendation: MANHATTAN FILE panel: a folder-styled drill-down (Courier Prime, stamp graphics, 'TOP SECRET — EYES ONLY' chrome). Left column: a vertical milestone ladder (ORE → SEPARATION → DESIGN → ASSEMBLY → TEST → STOCKPILE → THERMONUCLEAR → each delivery leg), each milestone showing exact % / date estimate and its binding constraint in red ('LIMITED BY: GRID CAPACITY, URALS REGION — 34 MW SHORTFALL'). Right column: named facilities on a mini-map (these are targetable/sabotage-able, tying to the intel pillar). Milestones complete via a teletype wire line, not a popup. No abstract 'research points' — the program should visibly eat uranium, megawatts, and industry, because economic systems competition is a pillar.

findings.name: Enemy programs: estimate dossiers that are honestly wrong, with confidence and provenance
findings.detail: The historical record is a gift: US NIEs predicted the Soviet bomb for 1953 (actual: 1949) ([RDS-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RDS-1)); NIE 11-5-58 projected 100 Soviet ICBMs by 1960 and 500 by 1961-62 when the real number was 4, and Corona imagery in 1961 collapsed the estimate to ≤25 because R-7 launchers were 'large and easy to spot' ([Wikipedia: Missile gap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missile_gap)). Estimates were not just ranges — they had provenance (air sampling, U-2, Corona, HUMINT), confidence, and staleness, and they moved in discrete jumps when a new source came online. The game already renders 'EST 25-45' fuzzed 2-sig-fig language; the nuclear layer is where that language becomes a core mechanic rather than cosmetics.
findings.recommendation: One ESTIMATE CARD per nuclear-relevant nation, styled as an NIE cover sheet: 'SOVIET ATOMIC PROGRAM — EST FIRST TEST: 1952-1954 — CONFIDENCE: LOW — BASIS: HUMINT, ATTACHÉ — AS OF: MAR 1950.' Under the hood the sim tracks truth; the card shows a band whose width and CENTER ERROR are functions of intel coverage — with a deliberate historical bias knob so estimates skew late on programs and high on arsenals (bomber/missile-gap paranoia) unless the player invests in overhead reconnaissance. New collection assets cause discrete revision events on the wire ('NIE REVISED: SOVIET STOCKPILE EST 150-300 → 20-45'), which are dramatic beats in themselves. Stale estimates visibly age (AS OF date turns amber, then red). Never show the true number, even in hindsight tooltips — only a post-game archive may reveal truth.

findings.name: Stockpile and reach: exact-vs-fuzzed twin arsenal panels, and reach as coverage shading, not ring clutter
findings.detail: DEFCON shows silos/subs/bombers with range indicators on the vector map and was praised for an 'elementary' uncluttered interface ([Defcon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defcon_(video_game))). But dozens of overlapping range rings are noise; what a 1950 planner actually cares about is 'which of their cities can I reach, and which of mine can they reach' — in 1950 that means bomber radii from real bases (SAC forward basing is the whole strategic question of the era), later missile arcs.
findings.recommendation: ARSENAL ledger, two columns, brutally asymmetric by design: OWN column exact ('STOCKPILE: 12 — MK-4 FISSION — ASSIGNED: 8 SAC UK, 4 CONUS RESERVE'); THEIR column fuzzed ('EST 0-5 — CONF LOW'). On THE BOARD map mode, reach renders as coverage tint, not rings: provinces inside enemy delivery reach get a faint red scanline wash, provinces you can reach get blue — the overlap zone is the brinkmanship map, readable in one glance. Individual range rings appear only on hover/selection of a base. Delivery is its own milestone row (bomber → forward basing → jet bomber → IRBM → ICBM → SSBN), because reach growing over the campaign is the visible arms race. Enemy coverage tint derives from the ESTIMATE, not truth — so a bad estimate literally distorts the player's map, which is the intelligence pillar earning its keep.

findings.name: The alert-posture lever: a player-owned control with weight, cost, and visibility rules
findings.detail: Real DEFCON is set from the top (president/SecDef via the Chairman JCS) and is NOT announced publicly — DEFCON 2 was reached only in the Cuban Missile Crisis, and levels are classified ([Wikipedia: DEFCON](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DEFCON)). Introversion's DEFCON makes the level a shared automatic timer, and Twilight Struggle makes it a consequence of actions. The design opening: make posture a CHOICE the player owns, distinct from world tension — tension is the weather, posture is your umbrella, and raising your umbrella changes the weather.
findings.recommendation: READINESS lever, always visible, bottom-left of the map: five heavy detented positions (5→1) drawn as a physical rotary/slide control. Raising it requires press-and-HOLD with an authentication beat ('CONFIRM — AUTH CODE ACCEPTED' teletype line) — never a single click; lowering is instant. Each step has printed, concrete effects on the lever itself: bomber dispersal %, response time, daily economic upkeep, accident/false-alarm event weight, and a tension delta. The whole UI chrome shifts with posture (amber wash at 3, red at 2, klaxon sting + heartbeat-slow ambient at 1) so the player FEELS parked at high alert and wants to come down — sustained high posture must bleed money and risk Broken Arrow / false-warning scripted events. Visibility rule: the enemy does not see your lever, they see detectable signatures (dispersal, comms volume) through THEIR intel, with lag and error — and vice versa: their posture appears on your board as 'EST POSTURE: 3-2, CONF MED', so misreading an exercise as mobilization becomes a playable 1983-Able-Archer failure mode.

findings.name: The first test: two completely different event presentations, and the detection chain is the better one
findings.detail: Joe-1's real-world reveal is a ready-made event script: a WB-29 sampling flight from Misawa to Eielson on 3 Sept 1949 caught the debris; confirmation took cross-referenced follow-up flights; Truman announced on 23 Sept — 'We have evidence that within recent weeks an atomic explosion occurred in the U.S.S.R.' — and the announcement itself blindsided Moscow, which hoped to keep the test secret and didn't know the detection capability existed ([RDS-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RDS-1)). The Doomsday Clock jumped from 7 to 3 minutes-to-midnight on that news ([Wikipedia: Doomsday Clock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doomsday_Clock)). That's four beats — detection, confirmation delay, disclosure choice, world reaction — all native to the game's teletype/choice-event engine.
findings.recommendation: OWN first test: the one earned full-screen moment in the game. Cut to black; Courier Prime countdown; single frame of white; then a seismograph trace draws across the screen and the wire prints the yield and the shot name the player chose. Follow immediately with a CHOICE EVENT: announce (tension +, prestige +, deterrence credibility +) or conceal (risk of enemy detection revealing it on THEIR terms). ENEMY first test: never announced by the sim directly — it arrives as the detection chain over several in-game days: 'AIR SAMPLING FLIGHT REPORTS ANOMALOUS RADIOACTIVITY — CONF LOW' → follow-up flights → 'CONSISTENT WITH ATOMIC DETONATION — CONF HIGH' → player's disclosure choice → estimate card lurches ('EST FIRST TEST 1952-1954' overstamped 'TESTED'), world tension band-jumps, Doomsday-Clock hand on the tension widget visibly snaps forward. If the player never built sampling flights, they find out from public sources, later and worse.

findings.name: The apocalyptic end-state: an unceremonious archive, not a game-over screen
findings.detail: DEFCON's whole thesis is that its endgame is a scoring of megadeaths in which nobody wins — play continues past DEFCON 1 until 80% of missiles are spent, then a timer runs out and the tally is read ([Defcon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defcon_(video_game))); WarGames states the genre's moral outright: after brute-forcing every scenario, WOPR concludes the only winning move is not to play ([WarGames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WarGames)). The design north star already says total war is the FAILURE state — so the screen must refuse every 'defeat screen' convention: no dramatic music swell, no 'try again' button in your face, no score.
findings.recommendation: When escalation crosses the threshold: the player LOSES CONTROL — inputs die, speed controls lock, and the exchange plays out on THE BOARD in real time at fixed speed, arcs crossing, province lights going out one by one, using the real province-level demography so the casualty counter counts actual modeled people. Audio: cut all music; leave only teletype chatter that gradually stops, then room tone. Then a plain typed page, Courier Prime on black — an armistice-document/after-action register: date, precipitating action AND WHO TOOK IT (attribution from the tension ledger), estimated dead as a fuzzed range even now ('EST 380,000,000-600,000,000'), duration of the war in hours. The final line before the (small, delayed) continue prompt: the hours the world stayed at peace under the player's stewardship — framing the whole run as 'how long you held the line,' which retroactively defines what playing well meant.

findings.name: Layout spec: what is always visible vs drill-down
findings.detail: Information hierarchy synthesized from the above. ALWAYS VISIBLE (every screen, every map mode): (1) top-center — the stepped world-tension track with band label and a small minutes-to-midnight clock face whose hand position is the poetic mirror of the band (the clock metaphor works because 'destruction will naturally occur unless someone acts' — [Doomsday Clock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doomsday_Clock)); (2) bottom-left — the READINESS lever with its current detent glowing; (3) the existing teletype wire, which is the nuclear layer's event bus (milestones, detections, NIE revisions, posture changes all print there). ONE CLICK away: THE BOARD map mode (coverage tints, bases, tracks) and the ARSENAL ledger. TWO clicks: MANHATTAN FILE (own program) and per-nation ESTIMATE cards. The tension track and lever must be adjacent-but-separate so the player physically sees 'world weather' vs 'my hand on the dial.'
findings.recommendation: Do not gate the tension track or lever behind the nuclear map mode — they are the pillar's heartbeat and belong on the default map. Conversely, keep stockpile NUMBERS off the always-visible layer (a number you stare at goes numb); surface arsenal only via THE BOARD and via wire events. Reserve the color red exclusively for the nuclear layer across the entire UI — no other system may use it — so any red pixel anywhere means 'this touches the bomb.' In 1950 the always-visible cluster starts nearly empty (no clock hand movement, lever capped at 4, board mostly dark) and the layer visibly wakes up as programs mature — the UI itself dramatizes the arms race arriving.

key_takeaways: The nuclear layer should be a PLACE (a dark vector 'BOARD' map mode with a docked console), not a set of windows — the entire canon (DEFCON, WarGames' HP-vector NORAD displays, Ken Adam's War Room) converges on the dark big board, and it fits the existing teletype/Oswald/Jost/Courier Prime identity perfectly.

Split 'world tension' (ambient, stepped band track + Doomsday-Clock hand, always visible top-center) from 'alert posture' (a player-owned 5-detent READINESS lever, always visible bottom-left, hold-to-confirm to raise, costly to sustain) — Twilight Struggle proves dread needs a chunky marker with printed restrictions and attributed movements; real DEFCON proves posture is a top-down choice that adversaries only see through lagged, error-prone intelligence estimates.

Asymmetric legibility is the core presentation mechanic: own program = exact stamped-dossier milestones gated by uranium, grid megawatts, and industry the game already simulates; enemy program = NIE-style estimate cards with range, confidence, basis, and AS-OF date that are deliberately, historically wrong (US predicted the Soviet bomb for 1953, got 1949; NIE 11-5-58 said 100 ICBMs, reality was 4) until collection assets trigger dramatic on-wire revisions.

Show reach as coverage tinting derived from ESTIMATES (their reach painted from your possibly-wrong intel), with range rings only on hover — a bad estimate literally distorts the player's map, welding the intelligence pillar to the nuclear one.

First tests: your own is the game's single earned full-screen moment (countdown, whiteout, seismograph, then an announce-or-conceal choice event); an enemy's arrives as the historical Joe-1 detection chain over days of wire messages — never as an omniscient popup.

The end-state screen must refuse defeat-screen convention: controls lock, the exchange plays out unskippably on the board against real province demography, audio decays to dead room tone, and a plain Courier-Prime after-action page attributes the precipitating action, gives casualties as a fuzzed range even then, and closes with the hours of peace the player sustained — defining the game as 'how long you held the line.'
Reserve red exclusively for the nuclear layer UI-wide, and let the always-visible cluster start almost inert in Jan 1950 so the interface itself dramatizes the arms race waking up.

reports.topic: Crisis and brinkmanship mechanics: the layer between the tension meter and general nuclear war

findings.name: Keep Kahn's thresholds, discard his rungs: a 7-rung crisis ladder
findings.detail: Kahn published a 16-step escalation ladder in 1962 and expanded it to 44 steps by 1965 in On Escalation (confirmed: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herman_Kahn). The 44 rungs are unplayable and were never the point — the load-bearing idea is the FIREBREAKS between groups: Kahn organizes the ladder into groups (subcrisis maneuvering, traditional crises, intense crises, bizarre crises, exemplary central attacks, military central wars, civilian central wars) separated by named thresholds — 'don't rock the boat', 'nuclear war is unthinkable', 'no nuclear use', 'central sanctuary', 'central war', 'city targeting' (Kahn, On Escalation, 1965). A crisis in our game should be an entity with a current rung 1-7: (1) Diplomatic confrontation/protest, (2) Show of force (fleet moves, mobilization), (3) Conventional engagement/blockade, (4) Ultimatum + nuclear alert, (5) Demonstration/first nuclear use, (6) Theater nuclear exchange, (7) General war = game over. Rungs 4→5 and 6→7 are the two firebreaks and must FEEL different: crossing 4→5 sets a permanent world flag `nuclear_taboo_broken` that changes all future crisis math for every nation; crossing 6→7 ends the game.
findings.recommendation: Implement `Crisis` as a sim entity: participants (two principals + clients), subject (province/country ref), per-side stakes (0-3 'vital interest' scale, asymmetric — Berlin is vital to the USSR, marginal to nobody), current rung (u8, 1-7), per-side commitment level, deadline in ticks, and a forked RNG stream `rng.fork(b"crisis:<id>")`. Rung transitions happen only through choice events (teletype presentation, which already exists). Never model the 44 rungs; model the 6 threshold-crossings as the dramatic decisions.

findings.name: Schelling's 'threat that leaves something to chance' as a per-rung autonomous incident risk
findings.detail: Schelling's core insight (The Strategy of Conflict 1960, ch. 8; Arms and Influence 1966): brinkmanship works because standing on the brink exposes BOTH sides to a risk neither fully controls — you don't threaten to start a war deliberately, you manipulate the shared risk of it starting accidentally. The mechanical translation: each crisis rung carries a base daily incident probability (integer basis points, e.g. rung 2 = 30bp/day, rung 4 = 250bp/day, rung 5 = 800bp/day), rolled once per in-game day off `SimClock::new_day` from the crisis's forked stream. An incident (patrol shoot-down, border clash, radar false alarm, a destroyer depth-charging a submarine) spawns a snap choice event with a 24-tick timer: stand down/apologize (credibility cost) or press (auto-escalate one rung). Modifiers to the incident rate: ongoing shooting war in-theater (+), hair-trigger posture of either side (+), predelegation doctrine (+), hotline/intel investment (−). The player's escalate decision is thus never 'start a war' — it is 'accept 8%/day that events take the wheel', which is both historically honest and mechanically legible.
findings.recommendation: Incident risk is THE core loop of a crisis. Display it openly for your own side ('Estimated risk of uncontrolled incident: ~8% per day') and let it be the number the player is actually gambling with. Deterministic: one roll per crisis per day, stable ordering by CrisisId (BTreeMap), all integer bp math.

findings.name: Commitment devices and a persistent Credibility stat (the Schelling 'burning bridges' economy)
findings.detail: Schelling: threats become credible by visibly removing your own option to retreat (tripwire garrisons, public ultimatums, mobilization you can't cheaply reverse). In-game: when escalating or holding, the player may attach a commitment rider — Public Ultimatum (broadcast, +2 commitment), Tripwire Deployment (move a formation into the disputed zone, +2, uses the existing military layer), General Mobilization (+3, economic cost via existing industry system). Commitment does two things: (a) multiplies the credibility/prestige loss if you later concede (concession cost = rung × commitment × stakes), and (b) is read by the opponent AI as evidence your threat is real, raising the chance THEY concede. Each great power carries a persistent Resolve/Credibility score 0-100: conceding under commitment drains it; honoring commitments restores it; it decays toward 50 over years. Low credibility means AI opponents discount your future threats — so a player who bluffs and folds twice finds crises stop resolving in their favor, which is exactly the Munich/deterrence-reputation dynamic. Balance of Power got this half-right: 'backing down in a negotiation results in a loss of prestige, which will reverberate politically' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balance_of_Power_(video_game)) — but made prestige the SCORE, which taught players to never back down. Credibility must be instrumental (affects AI concession math), not the victory condition, or you incentivize suicide-by-pride.
findings.recommendation: Own credibility shown exactly; opponent credibility and stakes shown only as fuzzed 2-sig-fig intel ranges ('Resolve: 60–75', 'They appear to consider this interest: VITAL?') using the existing intelligence-estimate display language. Better intel narrows the range — this makes the intel pillar directly feed the brinkmanship pillar: espionage literally tells you whether the other side is bluffing.

findings.name: AI concession model: deterministic expected-value with asymmetric stakes
findings.detail: Balance of Power's crisis engine worked because the AI's willingness to climb depended on the intrinsic importance of the disputed issue to it, and escalating over something the opponent considered vital was how you 'ignited a(n accidental) nuclear war... We do not reward failure' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balance_of_Power_(video_game)). Steal this: AI concedes when opponent_credibility × opponent_commitment × capability_ratio > own_stakes × own_domestic_pressure (all integer scales).
